ch4n1.title: A voice behind the door

questions.q: How can we tell that other visitors have already woken up the owner of the house before tonight?

options.text: He grumbles about "the very next time" and asks who it is "this time".
options.why: Clue: "the very next time this happens" and "Who is it this time". You only say "this time" if there have been other times.

options.text: He says the Rat has been knocking at his door every single night this week.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 5 he is surprised and delighted it's Ratty. He wasn't expecting him at all.

options.text: He says the heavy snow falling on his roof keeps waking him up at night.
options.why: Clue check: read paragraph 3 again. He is grumbling about people, not snow.

options.text: the snow
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: paragraph 3 asks "Who is it". A who is a person, not the weather.

questions.q: The Badger answers *in quite a different voice*. Why does his voice change?

options.text: Once he knows it's his friend Ratty, he stops being cross and is kind.
options.why: Clue: the gruff voice in paragraph 3 turns into "What, Ratty, my dear little man!" as soon as the Rat says his name.

options.text: A different animal from inside the house has now come along to the door.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 5 says "exclaimed the Badger". It's the same animal, just sounding different.

options.text: He has a bad cold, so his voice keeps going up and down all through the night.
options.why: Clue check: nobody in these paragraphs sneezes or coughs. Look at what the Rat says in paragraph 4 just before the change.

options.text: he is sleepy
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and it doesn't explain the change. Clue check: he was sleepy the whole time. What happened in paragraph 4?

questions.q: The Badger says *Why, you must be perished.* What does he mean?

options.text: He means they must be terribly cold and tired out from the snow.
options.why: Clue: he says it straight after "Lost in the snow!" Perished here means frozen and worn out, not dead.

options.text: He thinks they have died out there in the snow and are now ghosts.
options.why: Clue check: he tells them "Come along in, both of you, at once". You don't invite ghosts in for supper!

options.text: He thinks the Wild Wood animals have caught them and eaten them up.
options.why: Clue check: they are standing right in front of him, asking to come in. Nobody has been eaten.

options.text: frozen stiff
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: At the door, the Mole guesses what the footsteps sound like. What do we find out a little later that proves he was right?

options.text: The Badger's slippers really are old and worn down at the heel.
options.why: Clue: the Mole guessed "carpet slippers... down at heel", and paragraph 7 says the slippers "were indeed very down at heel".

options.text: The Badger is dragging a heavy lantern that bangs along the floor.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 7 says he carries "a flat candlestick in his paw". Nothing is dragging.

options.text: The Badger has hurt his foot, so he limps slowly along the passage.
options.why: Clue check: nobody says his foot is hurt. It's his slippers that make him shuffle.

options.text: floppy old slippers
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: How do we know the Badger was just about to go to bed when they rang?

options.text: He is in a dressing-gown and slippers, and carries a candle to light his way.
options.why: Clue: "a long dressing-gown", slippers and "a flat candlestick". That's what you wear and carry on your way up to bed.

options.text: He tells them he is already fast asleep and they should come back tomorrow.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 5 he says "come in with you". He never sends them away.

options.text: His bed is right next to the front door, and it is still warm from him lying in it.
options.why: Clue check: the story never shows us his bed tonight. Look at what he is wearing in paragraph 7 instead.

options.text: he yawns
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and it slips past the clue too. Clue check: nobody yawns tonight. Look at his clothes in paragraph 7.

questions.q: By the fire they are *now in safe anchorage*. What does that tell us?

options.text: They feel safe and still at last, like a boat tied up out of a storm.
options.why: Clue: the same sentence calls them "storm-driven animals" and says the Wild Wood feels "miles and miles away". Anchorage is where boats shelter.

options.text: They have climbed into a real boat that is tied up inside Badger's house.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 10 says they are sitting "on a settle to toast themselves at the fire". A settle is a bench, not a boat.

options.text: Badger's kitchen has lots of heavy iron anchors hanging from the ceiling.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 9 lists what hangs from the rafters: hams, herbs, onions and eggs. No anchors!

options.text: safe at last
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Find the moment the Mole starts to really like the Badger. What makes him feel that way?

options.text: Badger listens to their story and never once says "I told you so".
options.why: Clue: "he never said, 'I told you so'... The Mole began to feel very friendly towards him."

options.text: Badger tells them off for going into the wood, but then gives them cake.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 11 says he did not seem "surprised or shocked at anything". He doesn't tell them off at all.

options.text: Badger lets the Mole sit in his big arm-chair at the head of the table.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 11 says "He sat in his arm-chair at the head of the table". It's Badger's own seat.

options.text: he gives cake
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: it's not about food. Look at what Badger does NOT say in paragraph 11.

questions.q: At the start of tonight the two animals are stamping in the snow to keep warm. By the end, how have things changed for them?

options.text: They are warm and so full up that they don't care about anything.
options.why: Clue: "his skin was now as tight as was decently safe" and "he didn't care a hang for anybody or anything", sitting round "the glowing embers".

options.text: They are back home by the river, telling all their friends about the snow.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 12 they are still round "the great wood fire" in Badger's kitchen.

options.text: They are hungry again, because Badger only had a very tiny supper to give.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 11 says it was hard to know "what they should attack first where all was so attractive". There was plenty!

options.text: cosy by the fire
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Which word best describes how the Badger treats the Rat and the Mole tonight, and what is your proof?

options.text: Caring: he bathes the Mole's cut shin and fetches them dry clothes.
options.why: Clue: "he fetched them dressing-gowns and slippers, and himself bathed the Mole's shin with warm water".

options.text: Strict: he makes them wash all the plates before they can have supper.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 11 Badger lays the supper for them. Nobody washes anything.

options.text: Mean: he makes them sleep in the cold hall because they woke him up.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 8 says he takes them straight to "a large fire-lit kitchen".

options.text: Greedy: he eats up all of the supper and only gives them the scraps.
options.why: Clue check: Badger had already had his supper (paragraph 9). He lays a whole new one for his guests.

questions.q: Where does tonight's bit of the story end, and how is the Mole feeling?

options.text: By Badger's fire after supper, full and happy, as Badger asks about Toad.
options.why: Clue: they think "how jolly it was to be sitting up so late", and then the Badger asks "How's old Toad going on?"

options.text: Stuck outside in the snow, cold and scared that nobody will ever open up.
options.why: Clue check: they got inside way back in paragraph 6, "with great joy and relief".

options.text: In a little bed at Badger's house, too frightened of the Wild Wood to sleep.
options.why: Clue check: nobody has gone to bed yet. In the last paragraph they are still sitting by the fire.

options.text: very hungry
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: in paragraph 12 their skins are "as tight as was decently safe".

hints: Toad keeps crashing motor-cars, so the friends plan to sort him out when spring comes.
The Wild Wood animals surround the house, but Badger scares them off from his front door.
The Rat is desperate to get home, but the snow is too deep until the sun melts it.
The Mole gets lost in Badger's long tunnels, so Badger follows his squeaks to find him.

ch4n2.title: News by the fire

questions.q: The Mole *tried to look properly mournful*. Does he really feel sad about Toad?

options.text: No, he is too cosy and happy, so he is only putting on a sad face.
options.why: Clue: he is "basking in the firelight, his heels higher than his head". That's a very comfy, happy Mole. Tried to look means he is pretending.

options.text: Yes, he is so upset about Toad that he can't stop crying by the fire.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 1 says he is "basking" with his feet up. Nobody is crying.

options.text: Yes, he is sad because his feet are up so high that it hurts his back.
options.why: Clue check: basking means lazing about enjoying the warmth. Nothing hurts.

options.text: only pretending
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The Rat says counting Toad's crashes and counting his cars is "the same thing". Why?

options.text: Every car Toad gets ends up smashed, so the two numbers always match.
options.why: Clue: "This is the seventh", and the other six are in pieces in his coach-house. One car, one crash, every time!

options.text: Toad has lots of sewing machines at home that he keeps breaking by mistake.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 3 says the coach-house is full of "fragments of motor-cars". These machines are cars.

options.text: Toad has never once crashed; he just likes buying a lot of new machines.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 1 says "Another smash-up only last week, and a bad one."

options.text: every car smashed
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: How do we know Toad's crashes are really bad ones, not just little bumps?

options.text: His old cars are in bits no bigger than a hat, piled up to the roof.
options.why: Clue: "piled up to the roof with fragments of motor-cars, none of them bigger than your hat!" Only a huge crash smashes a car that small.

options.text: Toad has to buy himself a brand new hat every single time he crashes.
options.why: Clue check: the hat in paragraph 3 is just to show how small the pieces are. Nobody buys a hat.

options.text: Toad's cars all have little dents, so he parks them neatly by the river.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 3 says they are in "fragments", which means broken into pieces, not dented.

options.text: loud bangs
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and it slips past the clue too. Clue check: look at what is piled up in Toad's coach-house in paragraph 3.

questions.q: The Badger says he can't do anything about Toad right now. What does he say a little later that tells us when he will?

options.text: When spring comes and he wakes up fidgety, wanting to be up early.
options.why: Clue: "when once the year has really turned, and the nights are shorter" and he "feels fidgety and wanting to be up and doing". That's spring.

options.text: When Toad has crashed just one more car and learned his lesson at last.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 8 Badger talks about the nights and the year, not about Toad's next crash.

options.text: When the snow stops tomorrow and they can all walk over to Toad Hall.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 7 says animals don't do anything "strenuous" all winter. Tomorrow is still winter.

options.text: in the spring
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The Rat says "Not me!" when Badger says he is asleep. How do we know from what comes next that he really was nodding off?

options.text: The Mole laughs that the Rat has dozed off two or three times already.
options.why: Clue: "He's been asleep two or three times since supper," said the Mole, laughing. And the Rat wakes "with a jerk".

options.text: The Rat says sorry and owns up that he's been snoring all evening long.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat never owns up. He just says "Not me!" in paragraph 11.

options.text: Badger has to splash cold water on the Rat's face to wake him for bed.
options.why: Clue check: nobody splashes anyone. Read what the Mole says in paragraph 12.

options.text: Rat snored loudly
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and it slips past the clue too. Clue check: nobody mentions snoring. Who tells on the Rat in paragraph 12?

questions.q: Why is the Mole wide awake when the Rat keeps dropping off?

options.text: The Mole lives underground, so Badger's house feels just like home.
options.why: Clue: he is "an underground animal by birth and breeding", so the house "exactly suited him and made him feel at home".

options.text: The Mole drank lots of strong coffee at supper, so he feels too jumpy.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 12 gives the real reason, and it's about where the Mole comes from, not what he drank.

options.text: The Mole is still scared of the Wild Wood, so he wants to keep watch.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 12 says he feels "quite wakeful and even lively". Lively isn't scared.

options.text: feels at home
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The hedgehog says *mother would have us go, was the weather ever so*. What does he mean?

options.text: Their mother made them go to school, even though the weather was awful.
options.why: Clue: they were "trying to find our way to school". Would have us go means she insisted, and was the weather ever so means however bad it was.

options.text: Their mother wanted to go to school herself, but the weather was too bad.
options.why: Clue check: "have us go" means the children go. It's the hedgehogs who got lost on the way to school.

options.text: Their mother lets them go to school only on days when the snow falls.
options.why: Clue check: the hedgehog says she made them go whatever the weather. Snow isn't a reason to go, it's a reason not to!

options.text: mum is cross
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: the hedgehog is telling us where they were going, and who sent them.

questions.q: The storyteller says Badger was being *“busy” in the usual way*. What is Badger really doing?

options.text: He is having a nap in his arm-chair with a hanky over his face.
options.why: Clue: "settled himself in an arm-chair with his legs up on another and a red cotton handkerchief over his face". The quote marks round busy tell us it's a joke.

options.text: He is doing lots of hard sums at his desk and must not be disturbed.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 22 says his legs are up and his face is covered. You can't do sums like that!

options.text: He is busy digging a new tunnel to make his house even bigger again.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 22 says he is in "an arm-chair". No digging from an arm-chair.

options.text: working very hard
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and it slips past the joke too. Clue check: look at where his legs are and what is over his face in paragraph 22.

questions.q: Which word best describes the two young hedgehogs, and what is your proof?

options.text: Polite: they stand up, bow their heads and call the Rat sir.
options.why: Clue: they "rose to their feet, and ducked their heads respectfully", and the Rat has to ask them not to "sir" him so much.

options.text: Rude: they won't share their porridge and tell the Rat to go away.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 15 they stand up for the Rat. They are the opposite of rude.

options.text: Brave: they set off through the Wild Wood alone to rescue the Mole.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 17 they were going to school, and Billy "got frightened and took and cried".

options.text: Lazy: they lie in bed all morning and refuse to get up for school.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 17 they had set out for school in the snow. It's Rat and Mole who come down late!

questions.q: Where does tonight's bit of the story end, and how is the Rat feeling?

options.text: At breakfast, squashed in the Otter's hug, with his mouth full.
options.why: Clue: the Otter "threw himself on the Rat with an embrace", and the Rat splutters "Get off!" through his buttered toast.

options.text: In bed at Badger's house, fast asleep and dreaming of his river bank.
options.why: Clue check: by the end it is morning and they are eating breakfast in the kitchen.

options.text: Out in the snow, walking the hedgehogs home to their mother's house.
options.why: Clue check: in the last paragraphs the Rat is still indoors, eating buttered toast.

options.text: at the river
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: nobody has left Badger's house yet.

hints: Everyone at home thinks Rat and Mole are lost, so the Otter comes through the snow to find them.
The hedgehogs can't find their way home, so Badger sends someone to walk them back.
Badger is cross at being woken again, but a big plate of ham soon puts him in a good mood.
Snow has blocked Badger's front door, so they dig their way out with spoons until they see sky.

ch4n3.title: A visitor through the snow

questions.q: Why does the Otter come straight to Badger's house to look for the Rat and the Mole?

options.text: He knows that animals in trouble usually end up at Badger's place.
options.why: Clue: "I knew that when people were in any fix they mostly went to Badger, or else Badger got to know of it somehow."

options.text: He followed their footprints in the snow all the way to Badger's door.
options.why: Clue check: the Otter says "the snow had covered up all your tracks". There were no footprints to follow.

options.text: The hedgehogs ran all the way to the river and told him where they were.
options.why: Clue check: the hedgehogs are still in Badger's kitchen when the Otter arrives.

options.text: followed their tracks
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: in paragraph 1 the Otter says the snow had covered up all the tracks.

questions.q: The Otter says the robins hopped about *in their perky conceited way, just as if they had done it themselves*. What does he mean?

options.text: They looked so pleased with themselves, as if they broke the branches.
options.why: Clue: the branches "had been torn away by the sheer weight of the snow". The robins just look proud, as though they did it. Conceited means showing off.

options.text: The robins really did snap the branches off by hopping on them very hard.
options.why: Clue check: the same sentence says the branches broke from "the sheer weight of the snow". Robins are far too small!

options.text: The robins helped the snow to pile up by flapping their little wings.
options.why: Clue check: "just as if" means it only looked that way. The robins didn't really do anything.

options.text: little show-offs
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Why is the Otter so cross with the rabbit he meets in the wood?

options.text: Hundreds of rabbits could have hidden the Mole, but none of them helped.
options.why: Clue: "there are hundreds and hundreds of you... you could have taken him in and made him safe". The rabbit just says "do something? us rabbits?"

options.text: The rabbit was rude and wouldn't let the Otter sit down on his tree stump.
options.why: Clue check: the Otter creeps up on the rabbit. Nobody asks to sit on the stump.

options.text: The Otter wanted the rabbits to go and fight the Wild Wood animals for him.
options.why: Clue check: the Otter says they could have "taken him in", meaning hidden the Mole in their burrows. That's not fighting.

options.text: rabbit was rude
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: read what the Otter says to the rabbit near the end of paragraph 1.

questions.q: The Mole asks his question with *some of yesterday’s terror coming back to him*. Why does he feel that way?

options.text: Hearing about the Wild Wood reminds him how scared he was yesterday.
options.why: Clue: the same sentence says it came back "at the mention of the Wild Wood". Yesterday he was chased there.

options.text: He hears whistling outside and thinks the scary faces have come back.
options.why: Clue check: nobody hears anything outside. It's the Otter's story that brings it back.

options.text: He had a bad dream in the night about the rabbit getting cuffed.
options.why: Clue check: the Mole has only just heard about the rabbit this minute. He couldn't have dreamed it last night.

options.text: a nightmare
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: paragraph 2 says what brings the terror back: "the mention of" something.

questions.q: The Otter laughs when the Mole asks if he was nervous. What did the Otter say earlier that shows he really wasn't scared?

options.text: He came through the Wild Wood alone, and wished he had met Them.
options.why: Clue: he came "through the Wild Wood and the snow" and said "if I had had the luck to meet any of 'Them'". Luck! He wanted to meet them.

options.text: He brought the Rat's pistols and big cudgel with him to stay safe.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat still has his own pistols. The Otter never mentions bringing any weapons.

options.text: He kept to the river path and never went into the Wild Wood at all.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 1 he says "I came straight off here, through the Wild Wood".

options.text: he's fearless
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: How can we tell that Badger has just woken up when he comes into the kitchen?

options.text: He is yawning and rubbing his eyes, so he must have been asleep.
options.why: Clue: "the Badger entered, yawning and rubbing his eyes". Remember he was supposed to be busy in his study!

options.text: He is still wearing his red hanky tied round his neck like a scarf.
options.why: Clue check: nobody mentions the hanky tonight. Look at what Badger is doing with his mouth and eyes in paragraph 5.

options.text: He tells everyone he's just had a lovely long sleep in his study.
options.why: Clue check: Badger never owns up to sleeping. He talks about luncheon instead!

options.text: he's hungry
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and it slips past the clue too. Clue check: being hungry doesn't prove you were asleep. What is Badger doing as he walks in?

questions.q: Badger tells the hedgehogs *You won’t want any dinner to-day, I’ll be bound.* Why does he say that?

options.text: He is teasing them, as they have just eaten lots of porridge and ham.
options.why: Clue: they ate "oatmeal porridge" and the Otter called them "greedy young hedgehogs stuffing themselves with fried ham". I'll be bound means I'm sure.

options.text: He is going to tie them up so they can't eat any more of his food.
options.why: Clue check: bound here doesn't mean tied up. In paragraph 9 he gives them sixpence and a pat. Not very tied up!

options.text: He is cross that they ate all of his ham, so they get no dinner at all.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 8 says he speaks "kindly", and he sends someone to see them home safely.

options.text: they're too full
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The Mole tells Badger why he loves living underground. What does Badger say is the best thing of all, which the Mole didn't mention?

options.text: No weather: floods, draughts and storms can never reach you there.
options.why: Clue: Badger says "above all, no weather". Then he talks about the Rat's floods and Toad's draughty rooms.

options.text: No visitors: nobody like the Otter can ever find your door down there.
options.why: Clue check: the Otter found Badger's house this very morning, in paragraph 1.

options.text: No hunger: you can keep heaps of honey and apples underground forever.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 11 Badger talks about builders and weather, not food.

options.text: no rain
options.why: Right idea, but it's too small. Make it a full sentence, and remember Badger means all weather, not just rain.

questions.q: Which word best describes the Otter, and what is your proof?

options.text: Bold: he walks alone through the Wild Wood and laughs at nerves.
options.why: Clue: he came "through the Wild Wood and the snow" on his own, and says "I'd give 'em nerves if any of them tried anything on with me."

options.text: Shy: he is too nervous to talk to the Rat, so he hides behind the Mole.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 1 he tells a very long story, and he says he has "any amount to say to Ratty".

options.text: Lazy: he won't come to look for his friends until all the snow melts.
options.why: Clue check: he came through the snow "as the red sun was rising". He was up early to find them.

options.text: Timid: he hides in the rabbit's burrow the moment he hears a noise.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 1 it's the rabbit who is scared. The Otter creeps up behind him!

questions.q: Where does tonight's bit of the story end, and how is the Mole feeling?

options.text: At lunch, happy and proud, as Badger offers to show him round his home.
options.why: Clue: the Mole "assented heartily", and Badger says "I'll take you all round this little place of mine. I can see you'll appreciate it."

options.text: On his way home with the Otter, feeling nervous about the Wild Wood again.
options.why: Clue check: in the last paragraph they are still sitting at lunch in Badger's house.

options.text: In the kitchen, cross because Badger won't let him see any of the tunnels.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 12 Badger offers to show him everything.

options.text: very sleepy
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: the Mole agrees "heartily" in paragraph 12. That's lively, not sleepy.

hints: The Rat is desperate to get back to his river, so Badger shows them a secret tunnel out of the wood.
The Mole gets lost in the maze of tunnels, but he follows the smell of ham back to the kitchen.
The Wild Wood animals are waiting outside, but Badger says any friend of his will be safe.
The snow is too deep to walk home, so the Otter makes a sledge out of the old door-mat.

ch4n4.title: Tunnels under the wood

questions.q: How can we tell the Mole thinks Badger must have built all the tunnels himself?

options.text: He asks how Badger ever found the time and strength to do all this.
options.why: Clue: "How on earth, Badger, did you ever find time and strength to do all this?" You'd only ask that if you thought he built it.

options.text: He asks Badger to teach him how to build pillars and arches as well.
options.why: Clue check: the Mole asks a question at the end of paragraph 1, but it isn't about learning to build.

options.text: He tells the Rat that Badger must be the strongest animal alive.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat is back in the kitchen arguing about eels. The Mole only talks to Badger.

options.text: he is tired
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: look at the question the Mole asks at the end of paragraph 1.

questions.q: Badger says *It would be astonishing indeed ... if I had done it*. What is he telling the Mole?

options.text: He didn't build it; he only cleaned out tunnels already there.
options.why: Clue: straight after, he says "I did none of it, only cleaned out the passages and chambers".

options.text: He is showing off, because he really did build it all in one winter.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 2 Badger says "as a matter of fact I did none of it".

options.text: He is astonished too, as he has never seen these tunnels before.
options.why: Clue check: Badger is leading the way with his lantern. He knows these tunnels well.

options.text: not me
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Badger says the old city went "down, down, down". What went "up, up, up" after that?

options.text: Seeds grew into trees until the old city was under a wood.
options.why: Clue: "seeds grew to saplings, and saplings to forest trees". That wood is the Wild Wood!

options.text: The badgers built the city up again, brick by brick, even taller.
options.why: Clue check: Badger says the badgers only "helped a little" with the falling down, not the building up.

options.text: The river rose up and up until the whole city was under water.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 6 says streams brought "sand and soil", not a flood. Look at what grew.

options.text: the Wild Wood
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Badger says the Wild Wood has good, bad and indifferent animals, then adds *I name no names*. Why won't he name them?

options.text: He is too polite to say it, but he knows the Mole can guess who.
options.why: Clue: straight after, he says "I fancy you know something about them yourself by this time." The Mole met them yesterday!

options.text: He has forgotten the names of all the animals living in the wood.
options.why: Clue check: Badger has lived here for ages and says he'll "pass the word around" in paragraph 8. He knows them all.

options.text: He doesn't know a single animal in the wood, as he never goes out.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 8 he says "Any friend of mine walks where he likes". The whole wood knows Badger.

options.text: he forgot
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: read the very next sentence Badger says in paragraph 6.

questions.q: How can we tell the Mole still remembers how scary the Wild Wood was?

options.text: He gives a little shiver when Badger talks about the animals there.
options.why: Clue: "I do indeed," said the Mole, "with a slight shiver".

options.text: He refuses to go anywhere near the tunnel that leads out to the wood.
options.why: Clue check: at the end he goes through Badger's tunnel with everyone else.

options.text: He hides behind Badger's lantern and begs to go back to the kitchen.
options.why: Clue check: nobody hides. Look at how the Mole answers Badger in paragraph 7.

options.text: feeling chilly
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and it slips past the clue too. Clue check: this shiver isn't about the cold. What was Badger just talking about?

questions.q: Early on, the Rat and the Otter are happily arguing about eels. When the Mole comes back, how has the Rat changed, and why?

options.text: He's pacing about in his coat, missing his river terribly.
options.why: Clue: "the Rat walking up and down, very restless", with "his overcoat on". The underground air "was oppressing him".

options.text: He has won the argument about eels and wants to tell everybody.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 9 says he is "very restless" and anxious. Winners are happy, not anxious.

options.text: He is sulking because the Otter ate the last of Badger's fried ham.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 9 tells us why he is upset, and it's about the river, not ham.

options.text: wants to go
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Does the Rat really believe *the river would run away if he wasn’t there to look after it*?

options.text: Not really; he just misses it so much he feels he must go back.
options.why: Clue: "he seemed really to be afraid". Seemed tells us it's a feeling, not a fact. He's homesick for his river.

options.text: Yes, he thinks the river will dry up if he isn't there to fill it.
options.why: Clue check: nobody fills a river. The storyteller is showing how much the Rat loves it.

options.text: Yes, rivers near the Wild Wood run off if nobody watches them.
options.why: Clue check: at the end of the passage the river is still there, "the familiar old river".

options.text: it will flood
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: paragraph 9 says the underground air is "getting on his nerves". It's about how he feels.

questions.q: Badger says he doesn't want everybody to know about his bolt-holes. What does he do at the end of the tunnel that shows he means it?

options.text: He hides the opening with creepers and dead leaves.
options.why: Clue: he "made everything look as natural as possible again, with creepers, brushwood, and dead leaves".

options.text: He makes the three friends promise never to tell a soul about it.
options.why: Clue check: Badger says a "hasty good-bye" in paragraph 12. There's no time for promises.

options.text: He locks a big iron gate behind them and keeps the only key.
options.why: Clue check: read paragraph 12 again. What does Badger cover the opening with? It isn't a gate.

options.text: hides the hole
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Which word best describes how Badger treats the Mole in this passage, and what is your proof?

options.text: Protective: he says any friend of his may walk safely there.
options.why: Clue: "I'll pass the word around to-morrow... Any friend of mine walks where he likes in this country, or I'll know the reason why!"

options.text: Bossy: he makes the Mole carry the lantern and sweep the tunnels.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 1 it's Badger who "lighted a lantern" and leads the way.

options.text: Unfriendly: he leaves the Mole alone to find his own way back.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 8 Badger is "patting him on the shoulder". That's friendly.

options.text: Boastful: he says he dug every single tunnel all by himself.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 2 Badger says "I did none of it". That's the opposite of boasting.

questions.q: Where does tonight's bit of the story end, and how is the Mole feeling?

options.text: Hurrying home over the fields, glad he belongs in the countryside.
options.why: Clue: he is "eagerly anticipating the moment when he would be at home again" and knows he is "an animal of tilled field and hedge-row".

options.text: Deep in Badger's tunnels, wishing he could live underground forever.
options.why: Clue check: by paragraph 13 they are out on "the very edge of the Wild Wood".

options.text: Back in the Wild Wood, excited to go exploring all on his own again.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 14 says he "must keep to the pleasant places". No more exploring the Wild Wood!

options.text: back at home
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and it's not quite right either. Clue check: in the last paragraph he is still "hurrying along". He isn't home yet.

hints: The Mole smells his old home, but the Rat hurries on until he sees how sad the Mole is.
The river floods in spring, so the Rat and the Mole move in with Badger underground.
Toad crashes his car again, so Badger marches round to Toad Hall to sort him out.
The Mole gets lost again, but this time he knows the passwords, so he gets home safe.
